m1.intro: Welcome to the grid, tech. Safety first, always: this module teaches how current hurts people and hardware, plus LOTO, PPE and bench rules. You need 100% on the quiz, but you can retake it.
tips: It's current through the body that kills, not the voltage number on the label. Treat every circuit as live until you've proven it dead.
Lock out, tag out, then try to start it. Then verify zero energy with a meter you've just checked on a known source.
Capacitors hold a charge after power is off. Discharge them through a resistor, never a screwdriver.
mistakes: Assuming 'low voltage' means harmless.
Skipping the live-dead-live meter check.
Working alone on energized gear.
m1.celebrate: Safety cleared. You're officially allowed near live gear. Respect it.

m2.intro: Static you can't even feel can kill a chip, or wound it so it fails months later. Let's get you grounded and working inside the ESD Protected Area.
tips: Test your wrist strap every shift and log it.
Keep plastics, foam cups and regular bubble wrap out of the work area.
Move sensitive parts only in shielding bags or conductive totes.
mistakes: Wearing the strap over a sleeve instead of on bare skin.
Thinking a part is fine because it still works. Latent damage is real.
m2.celebrate: Grounded and guarded. No chip dies on your watch.

m3.intro: Tech math isn't calculus. It's prefixes, rearranging formulas and tolerances, the stuff you'll use every day at the bench.
tips: Learn the prefix ladder cold: p, n, µ, m, k, M, G, each step 1000x.
Use engineering notation (powers of 3) so you can read answers straight off a meter.
Sanity-check every answer: does 4.7 kΩ times 2 mA really give you 9.4 V?
mistakes: Mixing up milli (m) and mega (M).
Forgetting to convert mA to A before multiplying.
m3.celebrate: Prefixes locked in. Micro, milli, kilo, all yours.

m4.intro: Your first instruments: the DMM and the bench supply. Measure safely, measure accurately, and write it down.
tips: Voltage goes in parallel, current goes in series. Break the circuit to measure amps.
Move the leads back to the V jack as soon as you finish a current reading.
Set the supply's current limit before you connect the load.
mistakes: Measuring voltage with the leads in the A jack, which blows the fuse or worse.
Measuring resistance on a powered circuit.
Ignoring the meter's CAT rating.
m4.celebrate: Meter mastered. Measure twice, blow zero fuses.

m5.intro: Phase 2 starts here. Ohm's law and power are the core of everything you'll do. Master series and parallel circuits and the rest gets easier.
tips: V = I x R and P = V x I. Learn the triangle, then learn to rearrange it without one.
Series circuits share current and parallel circuits share voltage.
Predict before you measure. A big gap between the two is a clue.
mistakes: Running a resistor near its wattage rating, so it cooks. Derate it.
Mixing up an open (no current, full voltage across the gap) with a short (high current, near-zero voltage).
m5.celebrate: Ohm's law: mastered. V = I x R is now muscle memory.

m6.intro: Kirchhoff's laws let you solve any DC circuit: voltage around a loop and current at a node. Dividers are where you'll use them most.
tips: KVL says the voltage rises and drops around any loop add up to zero.
KCL says current in equals current out at every node.
A load on a divider changes its output. Keep the load at least 10x the bottom resistor.
mistakes: Losing track of polarity signs when you write the loop equations.
Ignoring the meter's own loading on high-resistance dividers.
m6.celebrate: Kirchhoff approves. Every loop and node, solved.

m7.intro: Know your parts on sight: resistors, caps, inductors, relays, connectors. The data sheet is your best friend.
tips: Color code: Bad Beer Rots Our Young Guts But Vodka Goes Well (0 to 9).
Check the polarity and voltage rating on every electrolytic and tantalum cap.
Read the absolute max ratings first. They're the cliff edge.
mistakes: Putting an electrolytic in backwards, which can make it vent or pop.
Reading an SMD code like '103' as 103 Ω. It's 10 kΩ.
m7.celebrate: Parts ID'd on sight. Data sheets fear you now.

m8.intro: Time to see signals. The oscilloscope shows what the meter can't: shape, frequency and timing. Let's lock the trigger in.
tips: Compensate your probe on the scope's cal signal before you trust any reading.
If the trace won't sit still, fix the trigger level and source first.
A sine's RMS is about 0.707 x peak. Your DMM reads RMS.
mistakes: Clipping the probe ground to a point that isn't ground, which creates a short through the scope.
Leaving the scope on a 1x setting while the probe is on 10x, so readings are off by 10.
m8.celebrate: Trigger locked. You can see signals now.

m9.intro: Caps and inductors fight change: one resists voltage changes, the other current changes. That's what timing, filters and transformers are built on.
tips: Time constant τ = R x C. A cap reaches about 63% in one τ and is basically full in five.
Reactance changes with frequency: a cap's drops as frequency rises, an inductor's grows.
A transformer's voltage ratio equals its turns ratio.
mistakes: Forgetting that a cap stays charged after power-off.
Adding reactance and resistance directly. Impedance adds as vectors.
m9.celebrate: RC, RL and RLC tamed. Time constants under control.

m10.intro: Semiconductors are one-way valves and electronic switches. Diodes, LEDs and transistors make circuits do things.
tips: Use the DMM's diode mode. A good silicon diode reads about 0.6 to 0.7 V one way and OL the other.
A transistor switch needs enough base current or gate voltage to saturate fully.
Always put a flyback diode across a relay coil.
mistakes: Running an LED with no current-limiting resistor.
Leaving out the flyback diode, which kills the transistor.
Handling MOSFETs without ESD precautions.
m10.celebrate: Semiconductors switched on. Diodes, LEDs and transistors handled.

m11.intro: Every device needs clean power. Follow the chain from transformer to rectifier to filter to regulator, and you can fix most supply faults.
tips: Troubleshoot block by block: AC in, DC after the rectifier, smooth after the filter, regulated out.
Use the scope's AC coupling to measure ripple.
Linear regulators need headroom, and they get hot.
mistakes: Probing a switching supply's primary side without an isolation transformer.
Ignoring a bulging filter cap.

m12.intro: Amps make small signals big. Op-amps follow two golden rules, and once you know them, most circuits read like a recipe.
tips: Golden rules: no current flows into the inputs, and with feedback the inputs sit at the same voltage.
Inverting gain = -Rf/Rin. Non-inverting gain = 1 + Rf/Rin.
If the output is stuck at a rail, check whether the op-amp is clipping or has no feedback.
mistakes: Expecting an output beyond the supply rails.
Forgetting the op-amp's power pins on a breadboard.
m12.celebrate: Gain achieved. Op-amps follow your rules.

m13.intro: Ones and zeros. Gates, flip-flops and counters are the building blocks of every digital system you'll ever touch.
tips: Build the truth table first and the circuit second.
An unconnected CMOS input floats. Tie it high or low.
Something stuck high or stuck low? Check for a missing pull-up or a shorted output.
mistakes: Mixing logic families without checking their voltage levels.
Leaving inputs unconnected.
m13.celebrate: Logic HIGH. Ones and zeros obey you.

m14.intro: Phase 3 is workmanship. It starts with the drawings, because if you can't read the documentation, you can't build or fix to it.
tips: Reference designators (R12, C4, U3) connect the schematic, the BOM and the board.
Check the revision letter before you build. Old revs cause scrap.
If the drawing and the hardware disagree, stop and report it. Don't guess.
mistakes: Working from an outdated print.
Counting pin 1 wrong on connectors and ICs.
m14.celebrate: Prints decoded. Schematic to board, no guessing.

m15.intro: Soldering time. Through-hole and terminal joints are the foundation of everything you'll build. Clean, hot, fluxed, fast.
tips: Heat the joint, not the solder. Feed the solder into the pad and lead.
A good joint is shiny (for leaded solder), concave, and wets both surfaces.
Clean the tip and tin it often, and use flux.
mistakes: Cold joints: dull, grainy and lumpy.
Too much heat, which lifts pads.
Moving the part before the solder sets.
m15.celebrate: Shiny, concave, wetted. Your through-hole joints pass.

m16.intro: SMT shrinks everything. Steady hands, good magnification and hot air make it manageable. Start big and work down to fine pitch.
tips: Tack one corner, check the alignment, then solder the rest.
Use plenty of flux and drag-solder fine-pitch parts, then wick off any bridges.
Bake moisture-sensitive parts if their bag was left open too long.
mistakes: Solder bridges between fine-pitch leads.
Tombstoned chip parts.
Overheating nearby parts with hot air.
m16.celebrate: Fine pitch, no bridges. SMT unlocked.

m17.intro: Quality is what separates hobby work from flight hardware. Learn the IPC classes and the target, acceptable and defect criteria, and how to spot defects.
tips: Class 3 is high-reliability work (aerospace, medical). Assume Class 3 here.
Inspect under proper lighting and magnification, the same way every time.
Document every defect. If it isn't logged, it didn't happen.
mistakes: Passing a joint because it works electrically.
Inspecting without a standard open to check against.
m17.celebrate: Inspector's eye online. Defects can't hide.

m18.intro: Wires carry everything. Clean strips, correct crimps and solid harnesses prevent a big share of field failures.
tips: Match the wire gauge, the contact and the crimp die every time.
Pull-test the crimp and check that the insulation and conductor sit right in the barrel.
Label and continuity-test every branch before you call the harness done.
mistakes: Nicked or broken strands from a bad strip.
Using a die that's the wrong size.
Over-tightening ties until they crush the insulation.
m18.celebrate: Crimped, laced, tested. That harness is flight-ready.

m19.intro: Phase 4: troubleshooting. This is where everything you've learned comes together. Use a method, not guesswork.
tips: Check the obvious first: power, connectors, fuses, smoke and smell.
Split the circuit in half, find the good half, and repeat.
Write down the expected value next to each one you measure.
mistakes: Swapping parts until it works, which is shotgunning.
Not retesting after the repair.
Skipping the write-up.
m19.celebrate: Fault found, fixed and verified. That's how a real tech works.

m20.intro: Final boss: build it, inspect it, test it, debug it and present it. Everything you've done leads here. Make it count, tech.
tips: Read the whole drawing package before you heat an iron.
Inspect as you go, not just at the end.
Keep a log of every problem and fix. The debrief scores that.
mistakes: Rushing the build and losing points on workmanship.
Not testing each subsystem before you integrate them.
m20.celebrate: Capstone complete. You built it, broke it and fixed it. Welcome to the crew, tech.
